summary.text: 次 is now used for “next,” “in sequence,” and “second in rank.” The oldest graph has competing interpretations: a military-station sign or a human figure. Manuscripts attest the ordered and ranked uses by the Qin and Han periods.

formation.text: The earliest construction is disputed. One analysis treats an oracle-bone form as a military-station sign, with an element identified as an early form of 師 and strokes marking an encampment. Other readings see a person exhaling or a speaking figure with possible saliva marks. Shuowen later analyzes 次 as 欠 plus 二, with 二 supplying a sound cue, but this does not settle the earlier graph’s construction.

components.text: In Shuowen’s analysis, 欠 depicts an open-mouthed or exhaling person. Other readings also propose a breathing or speaking figure, but do not establish 欠 as part of the earliest graph.
Shuowen assigns 二 a phonetic role in 次. A reported Old Chinese comparison shows similar final sequences, but does not establish that 二 was the sound element.

sound_limitation.text: The reported reconstruction comparison does not independently establish that 二 is 次’s phonetic component.

sound.text: In the Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese system, 二 and 次 have comparable final sequences. This comparison is associated with the phonetic proposal but does not establish 二’s role in 次.

components.text: In one disputed reading of an oracle-bone form, this element is identified as an early form of 師 and contributes to a proposed military-station scene.
In the same reading, two strokes mark an encampment or station. This proposed indicator belongs to that interpretation of the historical graph, not to the established modern analysis.

history.text: Oracle-bone and bronze examples are recorded, followed by Qin-slip, seal, clerical, and regular-script forms. One interpretation reads an oracle-bone graph as an early form of 師 with strokes marking an encampment, forming a military-station sign; other readings disagree, so the proposed scene remains uncertain.

Some bronze forms are described with marks below 欠 or short strokes, but their significance is unresolved. Shuowen later analyzed 次 as 欠 plus 二 and assigned 二 a sound role; this account remains disputed.

uncertainties.text: Interpretations of the earliest graph differ: proposals include a military-station sign, a person exhaling, and a speaking figure with possible saliva marks. These alternatives remain unresolved.
Shuowen’s analysis of 二 as a sound element is historically important, but the reported reconstruction comparison does not independently confirm that role.

No securely dated semantic path connects a proposed early meaning to “next” or “in sequence.” The lodging and tent examples come from transmitted texts whose witnesses are not dated in the cited accounts.

senses.gloss: in sequence; next or second in rank
senses.text: Qin- and Han-period manuscript citations attest 次 for ordered transmission and successive rank. These uses are established by that period, but do not show that they were the graph’s original meaning.
Transmitted texts use 次 for lodging or tents. How these uses relate to ranked and ordered meanings is unresolved.

A Han silk manuscript is reported to use 次 to write 恣. This is a separate word written with the same graph, not a demonstrated development of 次’s meaning; the proposed sound-based borrowing remains probable because the cited account gives no pronunciations to compare.

A Mawangdui manuscript is reported to use 次 where the transmitted Zhouyi has 濟. This is a separate graphic usage, not a demonstrated change in meaning; the proposed sound-based borrowing remains probable because the cited account gives no pronunciations to compare.

limitations.text: The Qin- and Han-period attestations do not establish the first occurrence of ordered or ranked uses, or their derivation from any proposed original sense. No semantic link is asserted where the evidence does not demonstrate one.
次 is reported in place of 恣 and 濟 in separate manuscripts, but the cited material gives no pronunciations to demonstrate or independently assess the proposed sound-based borrowings.

overview.text: 次 is now used for “next” and “in sequence.” The earliest graph is interpreted either as a military-station sign or as a human figure; its construction remains disputed. Qin- and Han-period manuscripts attest ordered and ranked uses.

components.text: In Shuowen’s analysis, 欠 pictures an open-mouthed or exhaling person; this does not settle the earliest graph’s form.
Shuowen treats 二 as a sound element. A reported comparison motivates that proposal, but does not prove 二 supplied 次’s sound.
One disputed oracle-bone reading identifies this element as an early form of 師, part of a proposed military-station scene.
In that reading, two strokes mark an encampment or station; this interpretation of the old graph remains disputed.

relationships.text: In Shuowen’s analysis, 欠 pictorially represents an open-mouthed or exhaling person within 次.
Shuowen analyzes 二 as the phonetic element in 次; this role remains disputed.
